chief_complaint: sudden excruciating pain and swelling in the left testicle for 2 hours
hpi_details: 21M college student presents with sudden, severe pain and swelling in his left testicle that began 2 hours ago. Pain is accompanied by lower abdominal pain and nausea.
expectations: wants immediate ultrasound and pain relief

core_concepts: Acute unilateral scrotal pain is testicular torsion until proven otherwise; salvage declines with ischemia time, so clinical suspicion requires immediate urology/surgical action.
A high-riding/transverse testis, nausea/vomiting, and absent cremasteric reflex increase suspicion, but no single sign—including Prehn sign—reliably excludes torsion.
Color Doppler ultrasound can support diagnosis only when immediately available and it does not delay exploration; normal/equivocal flow does not override strong clinical suspicion.
Definitive management is urgent scrotal exploration, detorsion, viability assessment, and bilateral orchiopexy; analgesia, NPO status, and surgical consultation must not await imaging.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating pain and swelling in the left testicle for 2 hours
Key HPI features: 21M college student presents with sudden, severe pain and swelling in his left testicle that began 2 hours ago. Pain is accompanied by lower abdominal pain and nausea.

Objective/Exam findings: Record onset time and vital signs; examine both testes for lie, height, swelling, tenderness, and cremasteric reflex. Obtain Doppler ultrasound only if it will not delay urgent exploration.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Testicular Torsion.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute epididymitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Waiting for ultrasound, laboratory results, or response to analgesia when history/examination is strongly concerning for torsion.
Ruling out torsion because Prehn sign is positive, the cremasteric reflex is present, symptoms are intermittent, or pain began more than six hours ago.
Treating presumed epididymitis and arranging outpatient follow-up before urgent surgical assessment of sudden scrotal pain.
Failing to arrange bilateral fixation during operative management because the contralateral bell-clapper risk remains.
management_principles: Activate urgent urology/surgical consultation, keep the patient NPO, establish IV access, and provide analgesia/antiemetic without delaying exploration.
Proceed to immediate exploration when torsion is clinically likely; use Doppler only when it is truly immediate and diagnostic uncertainty remains.
Counsel that manual detorsion is only a temporizing maneuver by an experienced clinician when surgery is not immediately available and never replaces exploration and bilateral orchiopexy.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Surgical emergency caused by twisting of the spermatic cord, producing acute testicular ischemia.

must_ask.say: Did this severe pain in your scrotum start suddenly, waking you up or while resting?
Along with the testicular pain, have you vomited or felt sick to your stomach?
Does gently lifting your scrotum ease the pain, or does it stay severe?
Did you suffer any hit or trauma to your groin area before the pain started?
Do you have a fever or burning when you urinate?
